text:
Outredgeous Lettuce Root Disease Diagnosis for Future Spaceflight
Evidence scope for space crop disease diagnosis

Haveman et al. developed a plant nucleic acid extraction workflow for future in situ disease diagnosis in space. They tested it at Kennedy Space Center using experimentally inoculated lettuce, tomato, and pepper. The study establishes a ground-based proof of concept for extracting plant and pathogen nucleic acids. Full automation and operation in a spaceflight environment remain future work.

text:
Outredgeous Lettuce Root Disease Diagnosis for Future Spaceflight
Root symptoms in Pythium-inoculated Outredgeous lettuce

Pythium aphanidermatum is associated with root rot in hydroponically grown lettuce. In the inoculated Outredgeous plants, the authors observed dark, deteriorating roots and extensive tissue necrosis. They grew healthy controls at the same time and kept them in a separate incubator to limit cross-contamination.

text:
Outredgeous Lettuce Root Disease Diagnosis for Future Spaceflight
Experimental inoculation and inconsistent sampling timing

The investigators inoculated 21-day-old Outredgeous lettuce roots with Pythium aphanidermatum in a silica-sand growth system. Section 2.3 reports harvesting infected roots 21 days after inoculation. Section 3.2 describes symptom development for 14 days after inoculation, and Figure 4A labels the pictured roots as 14 days postinoculation. These are experimental timings, and the source gives different timings for root harvest and the illustrated observations.

text:
Outredgeous Lettuce Root Disease Diagnosis for Future Spaceflight
Root sampling and DNA extraction limits

The researchers used approximately 1.2 g fresh weight of root material for DNA extraction from both healthy and inoculated lettuce. They ground the thick root tissue to powder with liquid nitrogen before processing it in the microHomogenizer. Softer material such as leaves did not need this extra step in the study. The authors identified improved homogenization of fibrous tissue as a design need for future use in microgravity.

text:
Outredgeous Lettuce Root Disease Diagnosis for Future Spaceflight
Targeted PCR detection of the lettuce root pathogen

Using semi-specific PCR primers, the researchers observed the expected 656 bp amplification product in the inoculated lettuce roots and in the cultured Pythium aphanidermatum positive control. The healthy-root sample did not show the same product. The result demonstrates detection of the target in the study's controlled samples.

text:
Outredgeous Lettuce Root Disease Diagnosis for Future Spaceflight
Reference database limitations for pathogen sequencing

The study's standard Kraken2 workflow did not identify Pythium aphanidermatum in inoculated lettuce roots because the relevant genome was missing from the curated RefSeq database used by the pipeline. Alignment against the target genome alone produced hits in inoculated roots and the pure culture. In a broader comparison with 420 oomycete genomes, the species was identified in the pure culture, with no species-level identification in inoculated roots.
